title: How an LED works
body: LED stands for light-emitting diode. A diode is a one-way door for current. Current goes in at the long leg (the anode) and out at the short leg (the cathode). Put it in backwards and it won't light.
A red LED needs a push of about 2 volts before much current flows. It's made for a small current, about 10 to 20 milliamps (mA). Its top limit is about 30 mA.

Above about 2 V, each extra bit of voltage makes the current shoot up. Wire an LED straight to a battery and the current rushes past its limit. Then the LED burns out. A resistor works like a narrow bit of pipe. It holds the current down to a safe level.
realWorld: LED lamps, phone screens and bike lights all have a resistor or a small driver chip. It keeps the current through the LEDs safe.
sources: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, §9.7 Semiconductor Devices. https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-3/pages/9-7-semiconductor-devices
